ch16.title: A Box of Precious Ointment
ch16.b002: The last week at the Pella camp was full of excited voices. The news that Lazarus had been raised had stirred up a fever the people had not felt since the feeding of the five thousand. Between the tents men told the same story over and over, and every time it was told it grew a little. Each afternoon the Master preached to the crowds, and each night he answered the questions of the apostles and the more advanced disciples.
ch16.b003: Simon Zelotes slept badly all that week. At Bethany he had watched the tomb opened. He had seen the body in its linen wrappings stand up. One thought had lodged in his chest at that moment and stayed there: that power was enough. Before a man who could turn back death, what were Roman swords, what was Herod’s army? He thought of his old comrades among the Zealots. They had called him a traitor. Now they would see. Every night Simon went out of his tent and looked at the southern sky. Beyond it lay Jerusalem.
ch16.b004: One evening Simon asked the Master about something he had said that day: that many children of the world were wiser in their generation than the children of the kingdom, because they knew how to make friends with the mammon of unrighteousness. The words bothered him. Were the sharp dealers of this world wise? The Master answered that some of them, before they entered the kingdom, had been shrewd in business, looking ahead to their own profit and safety. Should they show less diligence now in winning souls, when they had become stewards of God? Then he told them about a shrewd but dishonest steward who had wasted his master’s goods and was about to be dismissed, and who called in his master’s debtors and wrote down their bonds, so as to have friends when he was put out. Whoever was faithful in little, the Master said, would be faithful in much. And no one could serve two masters.
ch16.b005: Some Pharisees who were present began to sneer, for they were men much given to getting rich. They tried to draw the Master into a useless argument. He would not debate with them, and withdrew to his tent for the night. The Pharisees fell to quarreling among themselves, and as their voices rose, people from the camp round about crowded in. The noise grew.
ch16.b006: Then Simon Peter stood up. He raised his hands to quiet them and told them it was not fitting to dispute this way; the Master had spoken, and they would do well to think about his words. And he told them the old story of the Nazarites that John the Baptist used to thunder out, about the rich man and the beggar Lazarus. Peter’s voice was strong and clear. The crowd grew still. When the story was done, Andrew got up and sent them all off to their beds.
ch16.b007: Simon Zelotes watched and thought that Peter’s way with a crowd was something to see. If a voice like that rang out in the temple courts at Jerusalem. He held the picture in his mind for a long while. Judas Iscariot, a little way off, watched the same scene and reckoned something different. Peter again. Whenever anything happened, it was always Peter or James or John who stood in front.
ch16.b009: On Saturday afternoon, March 11, the Master preached his last sermon at Pella, a long address on the kingdom of heaven. The next day he announced that on the following morning he and the apostles would set out for the Passover at Jerusalem, visiting many towns of southern Perea on the way. As the word spread through the camp, faces changed. Jerusalem. The kingdom. The throne of David. No matter what the Master said about the unworldly nature of the kingdom, he could not erase from the minds of his Jewish hearers the dream of a kingdom set up in Jerusalem.
ch16.b010: That Sunday afternoon Salome, the wife of Zebedee, came to the Master with her two sons. As one might approach an Eastern ruler, she asked him to promise in advance to grant whatever she requested. The Master would make no such promise; he asked her what she wanted. Salome asked that when he went up to Jerusalem and set up his kingdom, her two sons might sit one on his right hand and the other on his left.
ch16.b011: The Master told her that she did not know what she was asking. Then he looked straight at James and John. He had known them and loved them a long time, he said; he had even lived in their mother’s house; Andrew had placed them always at his side; and because of all that, they had let their mother come to him secretly with such a request? Then he asked them whether they could drink the cup he was about to drink. Without a moment’s thought the two brothers said they could. The Master said it saddened him that they did not know why they were going up to Jerusalem. But because he knew they loved him in their hearts, they would indeed drink of his cup of bitterness and share his humiliation. The places at his right hand and his left, however, were not his to give.
ch16.b012: Someone carried word of it to Peter and the others. At first Peter did not believe his ears. Then his face went hot. James and John, sending their mother ahead of them, in secret. The ten boiled over all at once. The words grew rough. Peter was in the middle of it. He was not a man to hold his temper.
ch16.b013: The Master called them all together. The rulers of the gentiles lorded it over their subjects, he said, but it would not be so in the kingdom of heaven. Whoever wanted to be great must first become a servant. The Son of Man had not come to be served but to serve, and he was going up to Jerusalem now to lay down his life in doing the Father’s will and serving his brothers.
ch16.b014: To lay down his life. The apostles withdrew to pray. Peter went up a hill alone and sat down. His anger had drained away. Shame rose in its place. Could he say he had never coveted the right hand or the left? From the day he was first called on the shore of the Sea of Galilee he had always been at the front. He was one of the three who stayed close at the Master’s side. What James and John had asked for was not so different from what he already had. He had simply never said it aloud.
ch16.b015: That evening Peter went to the two sons of Zebedee. Then he went round to the ten, one by one. It was not easy. Simon Zelotes kept his arms folded to the end, and Judas Iscariot spoke softly but his eyes were cold. But before the night was far gone, James and John had made their apologies to the ten, and their brothers had accepted them. Andrew watched it all from a distance. He had known his brother could do this. No word of praise came out of him this time either. He only clapped his brother once on the back.
ch16.b016: Judas Iscariot lay in his tent that night and thought for a long time. The apology had been accepted. But what had that changed? The three were still at the Master’s side. They had asked for the right hand and the left, been reproved, and still had not lost their places. Judas recalled that he had never made such a request. He had always kept the accounts straight, guarded the purse, asked for nothing. And what had come back to him for it? He wrote the question into the ledger in his heart. An item still owing.
ch16.b018: On Monday morning, March 13, the Master and the twelve left the Pella camp for the last time. About a thousand disciples followed them. When they reached the Bethany ford of the Jordan, sometimes called Bethabara, a murmur went through the crowd. They had realized that the Master was not going straight to Jerusalem but meant to cross over toward Heshbon.
ch16.b019: The Master climbed onto a huge stone and spoke. Whoever wanted to follow him from now on, he said, must reckon the cost. A man who means to build a watchtower first sits down and works out whether he has enough to finish it. A king going to war first takes counsel whether he can meet twenty thousand with ten thousand. They could no longer follow along listening to the teaching and watching the works; they would have to bear witness to this gospel through bitter persecution and crushing disappointment. Anyone who sought honor and glory was like salt that had lost its savor. If they were not willing to drink with him the cup now being prepared, they should go back to their homes in peace.
ch16.b020: Half of the crowd left him at that ford. They went straight on up to Jerusalem. The other half, about five hundred, followed the Master toward Heshbon.
ch16.b021: Judas Iscariot looked up at the Master on the stone and weighed his words. Count the cost. He had been counting all his life. But the counting the Master meant was different from his. In the Master’s reckoning the side that lost was always the larger. Judas could not make sense of that arithmetic. No: he did not want to make sense of it. He watched half the crowd walk away. He knew why they were going. That the reason did not feel the least bit foreign to him made him uneasy.
ch16.b022: For more than two weeks after that they went round the villages of southern Perea where the seventy were working. At Heshbon the Master met Abner and told him he prayed the Father would give him wisdom to love and understand his brothers. That was the last time Abner ever saw the Master in the flesh. At every town some of the followers slipped away to go on to Jerusalem, until fewer than two hundred were left.
ch16.b023: The apostles knew that the Sanhedrin had sent word through all Israel that the Master had been condemned to die and that anyone who knew where he was should report it. And yet they were not so frightened as they had been at Philadelphia, when he told them he was going to Bethany. It was because of Lazarus. They had come to the conclusion that in an emergency the Master might use his divine power and put his enemies to shame. Judas held on to that conclusion harder than anyone. He had seen what happened at the tomb. How could a man who had seen that think of defeat?
ch16.b025: On Wednesday evening, March 29, on their way to Jerusalem, they camped at Livias. Simon Zelotes did not sleep that night. He called Peter out behind the tent.
ch16.b026: “The swords have come. More than a hundred of them.”
ch16.b027: Peter drew in his breath. It was a plan the two of them had laid together. Peter had not asked too closely where the swords came from or how. He had hesitated at first. But the leaders in Jerusalem had announced that they would kill the Master. If someone tried to harm him before he used his power, who would guard that short gap? Peter looked down at his hands. Hands that had thrown nets. That it did not seem strange to close those hands around a sword hilt seemed strange to him.
ch16.b028: They handed out the swords to all who would take them, to be worn hidden under their cloaks. Peter took one himself. The cold weight of the blade lay against his side. He did not tell Andrew. His brother would not ask. And Peter knew what Andrew would say if he knew. So he said nothing. Simon Zelotes looked round at the men wearing swords, and his face lit up. This was what he had waited for so long. The army of the kingdom. Small yet, and clumsy, but an army.
ch16.b029: Early the next morning, before the others were awake, the Master called Andrew and told him to wake his brothers; he had something to say to them. The Master knew about the swords. He knew which of them had taken one and was wearing it. But he never let them see that he knew.
ch16.b030: When the apostles had gathered apart, the Master spoke. In the trials ahead of them, he said, they were not to put their trust in the uncertainties of the flesh or in any human defense. And once again he told them plainly: they were going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man had already been condemned to death. He would be handed over to the chief priests and the religious rulers, who would condemn him and give him over to the gentiles, who would mock him and spit on him and scourge him and put him to death. But when they killed him, they were not to be dismayed, for on the third day he would rise.
ch16.b031: The sword at Peter’s side suddenly felt heavy. Do not trust in the flesh. The Master’s eyes passed over him. They did not stop; they passed over. Peter found that harder to bear. Simon Zelotes let the first part of the words slip by. He held only to the promise of rising on the third day. The third day meant soon. To rise must mean that the kingdom would rise. There would be a brief skirmish first, and then victory. That was how Simon read it, and most of the others read it the same way. None of them dared to ask the Master what he meant.
ch16.b032: After breakfast some friendly Pharisees came and urged the Master to get away quickly, for Herod meant to kill him as he had killed John. The Master told them to go and tell that fox that the Son of Man was preaching in Perea today, would go into Judea tomorrow, and in a few days would have finished his mission on earth and be ready to go up to the Father. Then he turned to the apostles and grieved over Jerusalem, the city that killed the prophets, whose children he had longed to gather as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, but they would not have it.
ch16.b033: Late that afternoon, Thursday, March 30, they came to Jericho. Near the city gate an old blind beggar named Bartimeus cried out to the Master at the top of his voice. People told him to be quiet, but he only cried louder. The Master stopped and told them to bring him over, and Bartimeus threw off his cloak and sprang out into the middle of the road. His eyes were opened. Near sundown Zaccheus, the chief publican, came down out of a sycamore tree, because the Master had said he would stay at his house that night. When one of the Jericho Pharisees muttered that the man was going to lodge with a sinner, Zaccheus stood up on a stool and declared that he would give half of all his goods to the poor, and that if he had cheated anyone, he would pay it back fourfold.
ch16.b034: Matthew looked at the little man on the stool for a long time. A chief publican. A name people spat at. And over that name the Master said today that salvation had come to this house. Matthew turned his head away and rubbed at his eyes. Simon Zelotes saw it. He said nothing. But that night, when they spread their bedding in Zaccheus’s yard, he put his down, for the first time, next to Matthew’s.
ch16.b036: They reached Bethany a little after four o’clock on Friday afternoon, March 31. So many people were coming every day to see Lazarus that arrangements had been made for the Master to stay with a neighboring believer named Simon, an older man who had been the leading citizen of the village since the death of Lazarus’s father. That night, while the Master slept, the apostles kept watch over the house in pairs. Many of them were wearing swords.
ch16.b037: Peter and Simon Zelotes stood the midnight watch together. Under the olive tree in the yard it was pitch dark, and now and then a donkey brayed or a dog barked at the far end of the village. Simon stood with his hand on his sword hilt, glaring into the darkness toward Jerusalem. Peter sat with his back against the doorpost, listening to the breathing inside the house. The Master was sound asleep. On the night the Sanhedrin had ordered all Israel to hand him over, he slept that peacefully. Peter envied that peace, and was a little afraid of it. He had come out to guard the Master, and it felt as though he himself were being guarded by that sleep. Early the next morning, though it was the Sabbath, hundreds of pilgrims came out from Jerusalem, and the noise woke everyone.
ch16.b038: On the evening after the Sabbath, a public banquet was held at Simon’s house. All of Bethany and Bethpage came. It was in honor of the Master and of Lazarus, and it was given in defiance of the Sanhedrin. Martha directed the serving. Mary, following Jewish custom, did not sit at the public feast but stood among the women who were watching. Agents of the Sanhedrin were there too, but they did not dare to seize the Master in the middle of his friends.
ch16.b039: Until he came to the table, the Master played with the children. He was unusually cheerful that night. He talked with Simon about Joshua of old, and about the walls of Jericho. He was not concerned with walls of brick and stone, he said, but he wanted to see the walls of prejudice and self-righteousness and hate come down. The feast was cheerful and calm. But all the apostles were unusually sober.
ch16.b040: Judas Iscariot sat at the end of the table with a cup of wine in his hand. He was reckoning up the evening: the whole village fed, the lamp oil, the mutton, the wine. Simon was a generous man, and Lazarus’s family was well off. That was good. The apostolic purse was always near empty, and the money from selling the Pella camp was still in David Zebedee’s hands. Judas had a rough idea of the sum.
ch16.b041: The feast was nearly over. From among the women who were watching, Mary stepped forward. She carried a large alabaster cruse in both hands. She walked straight to the place where the Master reclined as guest of honor and opened it. She anointed the Master’s head. Then she took down her hair, poured the ointment on his feet, and began to wipe them with her hair.
ch16.b042: The fragrance filled the room all at once, heavy and sweet and somehow cool. The smoke of the lamps and the smell of the meat sank beneath it. People fell silent. Lazarus said nothing.
ch16.b043: The moment the scent reached him, Judas knew what it was worth. Spikenard. Pure spikenard. A cruse that size cost a working man’s wages for a whole year. Enough to feed five thousand people. And that money was running onto the floor at this moment, down the Master’s feet, through a woman’s hair, into the cracks of the stone floor. The cup in Judas’s hand tipped.
ch16.b044: He heard murmuring. He was not the only one. Several people were saying it was a waste. Judas took courage from the sound. He got up from his place and went over to where Andrew was reclining, and spoke low but distinctly.
ch16.b045: “Why wasn’t this sold and the money used to feed the poor? You ought to speak to the Master and have him rebuke such waste.”
ch16.b046: Andrew did not answer. He looked up at Judas’s face. It looked righteous. The words were right, too. Feeding the poor was what the Master had always taught. And yet Andrew felt something churning beneath those right words. He did not know what it was. He was only bothered that Judas had come to him instead of speaking to the Master himself.
ch16.b047: The Master knew what they were thinking and heard what they said. He put his hand on the head of Mary, who knelt beside him, and his face was kind. He told them all to leave her alone. Why were they troubling her when she had done a good thing from her heart? To those who murmured that the ointment should have been sold and the money given to the poor, he said that the poor were always with them, to be helped whenever they wished, but he would not always be with them; he was going soon to his Father. This woman had long kept this ointment for his body at its burial, and since it now seemed good to her to anoint him beforehand, she was not to be denied that joy. By doing it, he said, she had reproved them all, for she had shown that she believed what he had told them about his death and his going to the Father. And wherever this gospel was preached in the whole world, what she had done would be told in memory of her.
ch16.b048: The room went quiet. Everyone had heard. The words were meant for all who had murmured. But that was not how Judas Iscariot heard them. To him they were meant for him alone. In front of everyone, the Master had taken the very words Judas had spoken to Andrew and thrown them out. And they had been words for the poor. The figures had been right.
ch16.b049: Judas went back and sat down. Nothing showed on his face. He was good at that. But inside him something was giving way, things that had been piling up for a long time. The Master who had left John the Baptist in Herod’s prison. The Master who had refused the crown when the crowd tried to make him king on the grass by the lake. The Master’s voice, the time he had gone to complain about Nathaniel, telling him not to make too much of his office. The three who asked for the right hand and the left and did not lose their places. All of it gathered now in one place. In the scent of the nard. He made up his mind to get even. With whom, he himself did not know. But at the end toward which that resolve was pointing stood the man who now had his hand on Mary’s head.
ch16.b050: He did not call it hatred. He called it justice. He always had.
ch16.b051: Simon Zelotes saw the scene from another place at the table. As the ointment was poured, his breath stopped at first. To pour oil on a man’s head was to make him king. Samuel had done it to David. Simon’s heart leaped. But the Master had called it burial. Ointment for the burial of his body. Simon wanted to act as if he had not heard that. He decided to remember only the oil of a king. Peter saw Judas come back to his seat. Judas’s face looked the same as ever. Peter thought little of what had just happened. He had been rebuked plenty of times himself. When he was rebuked his face went red, and then he forgot about it. Peter supposed everyone forgot things the way he did.
ch16.b053: On Sunday morning the Master called the twelve together in Simon’s beautiful garden. It was his last instruction before they entered Jerusalem. He would give many talks and teach many lessons before he went back to the Father, he said, but during this Passover they were to do no public work at all. They were to stay close to him and watch and pray. He knew that many of them had swords hidden on them, but he said nothing about it. Then he looked back briefly over their whole ministry, from the day of their ordination near Capernaum to this morning. The apostles listened in silence. No one asked anything.
ch16.b054: That morning the Master treated Judas exactly as he did on any other day. His eyes did not avoid him, nor did they rest on him any longer than usual. Judas felt it. And it tormented him more. If only the Master had taken him aside and scolded him. But the Master looked at him as though last night had never happened. Or was he looking at him like that knowing everything about last night? Judas could not be sure.
ch16.b055: Early that morning David Zebedee handed over to Judas the money from the sale of the Pella camp equipment. Judas counted it exactly. Not a coin was out. Then he placed most of it in the keeping of Simon, their host, against whatever urgent needs might arise once they entered Jerusalem. He did what a treasurer should do. Without a flaw. Judas noticed that his hands did not shake. That reassured him. He could still believe he was an honest man.
ch16.b057: When the noon meal was over, the Master called Peter and John. They were to go to Bethpage, he said; where the roads met, they would find the colt of an ass tied up. They should untie it and bring it back, and if anyone asked why, they should say that the Master needed it.
ch16.b058: Walking beside John, Peter felt laughter rising in him. At last. For the moment he forgot the heavy air of last night’s feast and the words of that dawn at Livias. The Master was going to do something. He was going to stand up before the people. In Bethpage, near a house on the corner by the open street, there really was a colt tied beside its mother. When Peter began to untie it, the owner came over and asked what they were doing. Peter answered as he had been told, and the man said that if their Master was Jesus from Galilee, he could have the colt. Peter took hold of the halter and turned to John. John was not laughing. He had the look of a man thinking something through.
ch16.b059: Meanwhile several hundred pilgrims had gathered around Simon’s house. David Zebedee and some of his former messengers, on their own initiative, hurried down to Jerusalem and spread the word among the pilgrims around the temple that Jesus of Nazareth was coming into the city. The twelve women of the original women’s corps arrived too, with some of their companions, and joined the procession.
ch16.b060: The Alpheus twins laid their cloaks on the donkey and held it while the Master mounted. Their two faces were equally bright. As the procession moved toward the summit of Olivet, people spread their garments on the road and cut branches from the trees to lay before him. And they began to shout hosanna to the son of David, and blessings on the one who came in the name of the Lord.
ch16.b061: Simon Zelotes was the loudest man in that crowd. He shouted himself hoarse. Pictures opened before his eyes. The Master reaching the temple and proclaiming the kingdom; the nationalists springing into action; himself in command of the new kingdom’s forces; the Sanhedrin and all who stood with it dead before sunset. The sword under his cloak bumped against his side. This was the day. He was sure of it.
ch16.b062: At the brow of Olivet, where the city and the towers of the temple came into full view, the Master stopped the procession. And he wept. A great silence fell. Simon’s shout died in his throat. In a voice thick with tears the Master said that if only Jerusalem had known, even on this day, the things that belonged to her peace. But now they were about to be hidden from her eyes. The day would come when her enemies would throw up a trench around her and leave not one stone upon another, because she had not known the time when God came to visit her.
ch16.b063: Simon Zelotes did not understand those tears. He had never seen a king weep on the day of his triumph. But when the procession moved on again and the pilgrims who had poured out from Jerusalem joined them waving palm branches, he began shouting again. Louder than before. As if to cover over those tears.
ch16.b064: Some Pharisees came up and told the Master to rebuke his disciples and make them behave more seemly. The Master answered that if these were silenced, the very stones by the road would cry out. Matthew heard one Pharisee jeer that everyone should look at the king of the Jews riding on an ass. He clenched his fist and only with great effort let it go.
ch16.b065: It was near the city gate. Out of the crowd a well-dressed man came up to Judas Iscariot and slapped him on the back. He was a prominent Sadducee, a friend of Judas’s family. With a gleeful face he asked why Judas looked so troubled, and told him to cheer up and join them all in hailing this Jesus of Nazareth as king of the Jews, riding through the gates of Jerusalem on an ass. Then he laughed and vanished into the crowd.
ch16.b066: Judas stood frozen. He had never shrunk from persecution. He was ready to be stoned, ready for prison. But this he could not bear. Ridicule. The men of Kerioth and Jericho, the friends of his father’s house, were laughing at him now: at the Galilean on the donkey, at the fishermen trailing after him, and at Judas Iscariot caught in the middle of them. For the first time he was ashamed of his Master. And that shame frightened him more than anything. That day the Master looked to him less like a king than like a clown. By the time the procession passed through the gate, Judas had nearly made up his mind to give up the whole idea of such a kingdom.
ch16.b068: While the twins took the donkey back to its owner, the Master and the ten apostles slipped away from the crowd and strolled slowly about the temple. Since getting down from the donkey, the Master had said nothing. There was no proclamation. No sermon. He only walked the courts, looking at the preparations for the Passover.
ch16.b069: Peter followed him and could hardly stand it. That crowd. A crowd so large and so ready to listen, and it was breaking up. He was burning to preach the kingdom right here in these courts, right now. But the Master had told them plainly that during this Passover they were neither to teach nor to preach. Peter kept his mouth shut. Keeping it shut was torture.
ch16.b070: As evening drew on, the crowds scattered to look for food. The apostles sat down for a while near the treasury and watched the people putting in their gifts. The rich put in a great deal. Then a poor widow in shabby clothes came and dropped two small copper coins into the trumpet-shaped box. The Master pointed her out to the apostles. She had put in more than anyone, he said. The others had given out of what they had to spare; she, in her want, had given everything she had, her whole living.
ch16.b071: Judas Iscariot heard the two coins fall. It was a thin, light sound. He was a man of figures. He could work out in an instant what fraction those two coins were of the cruse of nard that had poured onto the floor the night before. And twice now the Master had turned the figures upside down. Once he had called far too much the greatest gift, and once far too little. Judas hated that arithmetic. Before it, all his own reckoning came to nothing.
ch16.b072: The Master said that now they would go up to Bethany to rest. On the way back he walked ahead of the apostles. Not a word was spoken until they parted at Simon’s house.
ch16.b073: By five o’clock that afternoon Simon Zelotes had already become a man who said nothing at all. The one who had shouted loudest in the morning was the one most deeply crushed. He touched the sword under his cloak. It felt now like a useless lump of iron. The gloom that settled on him that day did not lift for a long time.
ch16.b074: The others swallowed that day each in his own way. Philip, as they neared the temple, had been seized by the fear that the Master might tell him to feed that crowd. So when the Master turned slowly away from the multitude, at the very moment the others were disappointed, he quietly let out his breath. Only after that did he, like Peter, feel sorry that nothing had been done to teach the people. Nathaniel had worked it out on the road already. Without so loud an entry, the Master would have been arrested the moment he set foot in the city. So he was not surprised that the Master made no further use of the crowds. Thomas followed along all day bewildered, thinking the whole thing a little childish. But by bedtime he had worked out that the Master had frightened the Sanhedrin so that they would not dare to lay hands on him at once, and the cleverness of it struck him as somehow funny, and he chuckled to himself. James Zebedee lay down in distress, never having understood the day at all, and John, remembering the prophecy of Zechariah, guessed a little at the meaning of the colt. Matthew, by nightfall, was worn out.
ch16.b075: Peter had regained his composure, but he was sad beyond words. He could not make out at all what the Master meant to do. That night he stayed with the Master and John at Simon’s house. Lying down, he unbuckled the sword from his waist and laid it beside his head. Then he remembered the words he had heard at dawn in Livias. Do not trust in the flesh. He picked the sword up again and hid it under his cloak. He did not throw it away.
ch16.b076: Only the twins were different. They came back late from returning the donkey and were puzzled by their companions’ downcast faces. To them it had been a perfect day from start to finish, the day they came nearest to heaven on earth. The two lay down side by side and were soon asleep. They were the only ones who slept much that night.
ch16.b077: Judas Iscariot lay on the floor of a friend’s house in Bethpage and stared at the ceiling. Should he just leave? he thought. Then he thought of Lazarus. Of the body walking out of the tomb. And he thought of the money. He could not desert with the apostles’ funds in his keeping. He was an honest man. So he decided to stay with the twelve for at least one more day. That was what he told himself that night. One more day. That night all the apostles were equally downcast and silent, and so no one found anything strange in Judas’s silence.
ch16.b079: The course of events follows Papers 169 through 172: the last week at the Pella camp and the excitement over Lazarus (169:0.1–0.2); Simon Zelotes’ question and the parable of the unjust steward, the Pharisees’ sneering, Peter quieting the crowd with the story of the rich man and Lazarus, and Andrew dismissing them (169:2.1–3.3); the last sermon on March 11 and the announcement of the journey to Jerusalem (170:0.1, 171:0.1–0.3); Salome’s request, the anger of the ten, and the reconciliation brought about by Peter (171:0.4–0.6); the departure from Pella on March 13, the sermon on “Counting the Cost” at the Bethany ford and the half of the crowd that left, the farewell to Abner at Heshbon, the shrinking of the company to fewer than two hundred, and the change from fear to expectancy because of Lazarus (171:1.1–3.5); the swords at Livias and the warning the next dawn, the word about Herod, Bartimeus and Zaccheus (171:4.1–6.4); the arrival at Bethany on March 31, the armed night watch, and the Sabbath pilgrims (172:0.1–0.3); the feast at Simon’s house, Mary’s anointing, Judas’s words to Andrew, Jesus’ answer, Judas’s resolve to get even, and the cost of the ointment (172:1.1–1.9); the Sunday-morning instructions and the funds David gave to Judas and Judas left with Simon (172:2.1–2.3); Peter and John fetching the colt, the twins’ cloaks, the procession and the hosannas, the tears on the brow of Olivet, the Pharisees’ protest, the Sadducee friend’s ridicule, the walk about the temple and the widow’s two mites, the silent return to Bethany, and each apostle’s reaction (172:3.1–5.13).
ch16.b080: Character details come from Paper 139: Judas mobilizing a lifetime’s resentment when his public protest was disallowed, and resolving to get even with he knew not whom (139:12.10); his being a poor loser who misread his friends and nursed grudges (139:12.6); the reproof he received after complaining about Nathaniel (139:6.5); his resentment of the three closest apostles and his belief that Jesus was afraid to assert his power (139:12.4, 177:4.4); his honesty with money to the end (139:12.3, 12.5); and Andrew’s reluctance to praise (139:1.10).
ch16.b081: Added as fiction are the apostles’ inner thoughts and feelings; the scent of the ointment and the sights and sounds of the feast; the brief words between Simon Zelotes and Peter at Livias; Peter laying his sword by his head and then hiding it again; Andrew clapping his brother on the back; Simon Zelotes laying his bedding beside Matthew’s at Zaccheus’s house; and Judas lying awake in a friend’s house. Judas’s words to Andrew keep the sense of the text in new words. The text says only that the apostles lodged with friends in Bethany and Bethpage, so Judas’s night is placed in Bethpage.
ch16.b082: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
